news.2026-10-30-israel-elections-aucune-: Israel: Likud comes first, but neither camp has a majority and Arab parties nearly double their seats
The final count gives Likud 27 seats, Netanyahu's bloc 53 and the opposition 48, out of 120. It takes 61 to govern.
The vote count is over: Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud remains the largest party, with 27 of 120 seats (20.5% of the vote) [1][3][4].
Netanyahu's bloc totals 53 seats and the opposition 48, so neither reaches the 61 seats needed to form a government [2][4]. Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar party wins 21 [4].

Arab parties won 19 seats (11 for the Joint List, 8 for Ra'am), up from 10 in the outgoing Parliament [2][4]. Official results are due to go to President Isaac Herzog on 4 November, and lawmakers will be sworn in on 10 November [2].
Key point: with no clear majority, Israel enters a period of negotiations that could last weeks, in the middle of a regional war [2][4].

Neither camp can govern alone: it will take either an unlikely deal between the blocs or a minority government that still wins a confidence vote in Parliament [4]. Until this is settled, budget and military decisions remain uncertain.
This vote changes nothing in your daily life right away, but the neighbour of Gaza, Lebanon and Iran may not have a stable government for several weeks [2][4].

news.2026-10-30-royaume-uni-budget-heale: United Kingdom: a first Budget with no surprises, taxed banks and a shrinking safety margin
New finance minister John Healey promises no extra tax for “working people” and makes banks pay. The state's safety margin falls to about £15 billion.

On 28 October, John Healey presented his first Budget as finance minister. He promised no tax rises for “working people”, helped households and drivers hit by higher energy prices, and raised taxes on banks [1][3].
The independent budget watchdog (OBR) puts the state's safety margin at about £15 billion in 2029-2030, against £24 billion forecast in March [1][2].

Markets barely reacted: the rate at which the British state borrows over 10 years hovered around 5.3% and the pound moved little [1][2]. A leak about the tax on banks still led the Treasury Committee chair, Meg Hillier, to write to the ministry and the financial regulator [3].
Key point: the Budget calmed markets, but with a thinner margin, any shock (energy, interest rates) could force the government to raise taxes or cut spending [1][2].
Analysts also note it contains no new measure to boost long-term growth [1]. The country already borrows at a high cost: around 5.3% over 10 years [1].
If you have savings or a loan in pounds, calm markets avoid an immediate shock, but the heavier tax on banks may eventually be passed on to their services [1][3].

news.2026-10-30-tanzanie-gaz-mnazi-bay-p: Tanzania: a new gas pocket of 223 billion cubic feet, ready to produce as early as November
The government announces 223 billion cubic feet of gas at Mnazi Bay, in the south. Operator Maurel & Prom says 200 billion, with first production as early as November.
Tanzania says it has discovered about 223 billion cubic feet of natural gas at Mnazi Bay, in the Mtwara region in the south of the country [1][2].
French operator Maurel & Prom, which drilled the Kasa-1X well with state company TPDC, instead speaks of about 200 billion cubic feet gross, about 120 billion of it its own share [1][2].
Production could start as early as November 2026, at about 50 million cubic feet a day [1][2]. The government puts its existing reserves at 57.54 trillion cubic feet [1].
Key point: with gas prices high because of the war around Hormuz, a country that can produce quickly becomes a card to play [1][2].

The gap between 223 and 200 billion comes from who is counting: the government announces an estimated volume, the company gives its gross figure and its share [1][2]. Official measurements will be needed to settle it.
This gas serves Tanzania and its neighbours first, but every new field outside the Gulf slightly reduces the world's dependence on Hormuz, which eventually weighs on your energy bill [1][2].

news.2026-10-30-bresil-petrobras-record-: Brazil: Petrobras breaks its production record, up 11.7% in a year, as oil is expensive
The state oil company produces 3.5 million barrels of oil equivalent a day in the third quarter, its highest level ever.
Petrobras reports record own production of 3.512 million barrels of oil equivalent a day in the third quarter, 11.7% more than a year earlier [1][2].
Output from the fields it operates also hits a record, at 5.08 million barrels a day, of which 4.46 million come from fields under the salt layer (the “pre-salt”) [1].
The previous record dated from the second quarter of 2026 (3.34 million barrels a day) [1][2].
Key point: while the Gulf is blocked, Brazil is producing and selling more oil, and gaining importance for countries looking for other suppliers [1][2].
The figure covers oil and gas, expressed in “barrels of oil equivalent”; for oil alone, estimates are lower (about 2.9 million barrels a day) [2].
Every barrel produced outside the Gulf helps calm fuel prices a little, though the effect stays small while the Strait of Hormuz is closed [1][2].

news.2026-10-30-ormuz-petrole-114-shell-: Shell's boss says it: oil at $115 is no longer “temporary”, because stocks are nearly empty
Brent ends around $115, on course for a fourth monthly rise. Iran promises to clear the strait in seven days, but Washington is weighing a return to strikes.

On 29 October, Brent closed around $114.88 a barrel and US oil (WTI) at about $102; on the morning of the 30th, Brent was rising towards $116 and finishing October nearly 11% higher, a fourth monthly rise in a row [1][2][3].

Shell's chief executive, Wael Sawan, said prices no longer look temporary, because global stocks are very low [1][3]. Europe has pledged to release 42 million barrels from its reserves over three months [1][3].

Iran says it expects to launch within a week a seven-day plan to clear the strait, but according to the Wall Street Journal a top commander briefed Donald Trump on military options, and he could resume strikes after the US midterm elections next week [1][2]. A tanker was also hit by an unidentified object as it left the strait [1][3].
Key point: as long as the strait stays blocked, the price does not fall, and even good diplomatic news is quickly wiped out by the risk of renewed strikes [1][2].
Traffic tracking shows only 2 transits on 25 October, against 85 a day before the crisis [3]. Price figures vary by contract and time of day; the orders of magnitude agree.
If oil stays at this level, petrol and heating oil weigh on your budget for longer [1][3].
